video_title: Blockchain Is Fixing a $2 Trillion Banking Problem with Mike Manning, Juan Montero and Anant
gist: A panel with Avalanche's Mike Manning, Fence Finance CEO Juan Montero and Grove's Anant argues that asset-backed finance and private credit — a $2trn market still run on spreadsheets, PDFs and emails — is the first asset class where blockchain rails deliver hard economics: ~80% operational cost savings and 30-40% cost-of-capital savings, with a live BBVA warehouse facility cited as proof. The core thesis is that today's tokenization is mostly digital-twin repackaging, and the real unlock is natively on-chain origination plus on-chain life-cycle management, which would have structurally prevented the First Brands/Tricolor double-pledging collapses. All three agree the binding constraint is institutional will and legal plumbing, not technology.

insights.claim: Private credit is a roughly $2 trillion market whose operations still run on spreadsheets, PDFs and emails, with settlement occurring weekly or monthly and reporting quarterly, despite financing credit card receivables, auto loans, invoice finance and merchant cash advances across the real economy.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: The gap between the size of the asset class and the primitiveness of its operating stack is the addressable market for private-credit infrastructure vendors — size the opportunity off operational spend, not AUM fees.
insights.quote: Private credit is two trillion dollar market and what surprises people is that this market still runs on spreadsheets, PDFs and emails.

insights.claim: Moving private-credit facility operations from manual processes into software delivers roughly 80% savings in operational cost and up to 40% savings in cost of capital, according to Fence Finance's observed deployments.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: These are the headline economics any private-credit tokenization pitch will be benchmarked against; if competing platforms cannot show similar cost-of-capital deltas, they are selling reporting software, not balance-sheet economics.
insights.quote: We're seeing 80% savings in operational cost. So in timings, as well as up to 40% savings in cost of capital by improving that efficiency.

insights.claim: The hidden cost of manual private-credit operations is not just headcount but negative carry: payments land one week to one month after they were due because reports, borrowing base certificates and covenant compliance checks must be assembled and reconciled by hand, creating idle cash and cash drag.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: Cost-of-capital savings in tokenized credit come mostly from eliminating float and idle cash rather than headcount — a durable, quantifiable line item lenders can underwrite.

insights.claim: Because reporting is periodic rather than continuous, private credit lenders structurally lack visibility into portfolio performance between reporting dates, which is where problems go unnoticed.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: Real-time portfolio visibility is the feature institutional allocators actually buy; treat monitoring latency as a credit risk factor when assessing private-credit exposures.

insights.claim: Asset-backed finance is the asset category best suited to web3 adoption because blockchain rails directly address its three primary risk vectors — fraud, double pledging and settlement risk — rather than offering a generic efficiency story.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: A clean screening framework: back tokenization ventures that map to one of these three pain points and discount those that don't.
insights.quote: this is the asset category best suited for the adoption of web 3 technology and the reason is that it solves the three primary risk vectors and pain points of this asset class in particular which are fraud, double pledging and settlement risk

insights.claim: Fraud in asset-backed lending can be eliminated by having the obligor digitally sign and attest to the underlying loan, making the document's integrity provable to third parties without relying on the originator's word.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Obligor-level attestation is the technical prerequisite for verifiable loan tapes — a diligence question to ask any tokenized-credit platform.

insights.claim: Blockchain settlement removes counterparty and cost layers by letting the obligor pay the current financial owner of the loan directly, without routing through the originator's bank account or a lock box.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Disintermediating lock-box providers and originator cash accounts is a direct margin transfer — watch incumbent trustee and servicer economics.

insights.claim: Securitization is inherently composable finance that has never had a composable technology stack — the loan, the warehouse facility and the securitized notes are linked layers that traditional finance can only reconcile manually.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Framing tokenization as delivering the missing composable stack for an already-composable product is the argument most likely to land with credit bankers — a useful lens for evaluating go-to-market credibility.
insights.quote: Asset back finance and securization is composable finance without a composable stack.

themes.theme: First Brands, Tricolor and the double-pledge problem

insights.claim: The First Brands and Tricolor collapses happened because the same assets were pledged into two different loan pools simultaneously, and 30-, 60- and 90-day lags in applying cash payments to specific loans meant unsynchronized systems let the scheme persist for a long time.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Cash-to-loan application latency, not credit quality, was the enabling condition for these blowups — screen private-credit lenders on reconciliation frequency as a fraud-detection proxy.
insights.quote: the systems were not synchronized. So even though the loan was issued and the loan should have been repaying, the lack of an immediate linkage between cash and loan activity allowed this to persist for quite a while in kind of a Ponzi scheme.

insights.claim: Tokenizing an asset does not prevent double pledging if the token is a digital twin — the same asset can be pledged on-chain and again in a traditional facility, so only natively on-chain origination where the loan documents name the blockchain as the control location closes the loophole.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: The most important diligence question on any RWA product: is this natively issued on chain with legal docs referencing the chain, or a twin that carries the same fraud risk as paper?

insights.claim: Avalanche's private-credit strategy rests on four pillars — legal enforceability, fiat-to-digital-cash ramps, ratings, and capital — with platform partners including Fence, Trunch and Tear, and allocators like Grove.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Ratings and fiat ramps are the least-built pillars; the appearance of a large rated on-chain deal would be the concrete signal that this thesis is inflecting.

themes.theme: Capital velocity and the capital-light originator

insights.claim: If loans are originated on chain and money moves on chain, an originator can pledge loan by loan instead of warehousing a week's production, collapsing its balance sheet requirement from a week's worth of origination to a single loan's worth.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: This is the clearest quantifiable ROE improvement in the whole thesis — a fintech lender's equity requirement falls by roughly the ratio of a week's production to one loan.
insights.quote: Now my balance sheet as an originator drops from a week's worth of production to one loan's worth of production.

insights.claim: Instant conditional funding turns fintech lending from a capital-intensive to a capital-light model, and makes economically viable assets with one- to three-day duration that could never survive traditional warehouse settlement lags.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: Watch for entirely new short-duration credit products (trade and acquisition finance, sub-week receivables) that only become financeable once settlement is instantaneous.
insights.quote: it turns a capital inensive model into a capital light model

insights.claim: Collapsing the money rail and the asset rail onto the same technology stack is the actual source of the efficiency gain, because it removes the gap between asset creation and cash movement that forces originators to balance-sheet production.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Use 'do money and assets settle on the same rail?' as the test that separates real capital-efficiency plays from reporting-layer tokenization.
insights.quote: collapsing the money rail and the asset rail on the same tech stack and what that unlocks is very very significantly accelerated capital velocity

insights.claim: Grove moved from tokenized treasury bills to placing roughly $250 million of Janus Henderson AAA CLOs on Avalanche as a way to bring off-chain yield on chain and dampen the volatility of crypto-backed lending markets.
insights.speaker: Anant (investments and product, Grove)
insights.so_what: Real-world credit is being used as a volatility dampener for on-chain lending rates — a structural, growing bid for short-duration institutional credit product from crypto balance sheets.

insights.claim: Grove's key capital-efficiency innovation is borrowing alongside its investments rather than sequentially: instead of buying the first $100 of assets then borrowing $98, it contributes $2 of equity and draws the senior debt simultaneously via codified smart contracts.
insights.speaker: Anant (investments and product, Grove)
insights.so_what: Simultaneous equity-and-senior deployment removes drag at the fund level and is a replicable structure for any levered on-chain credit allocator.

insights.claim: There are two distinct kinds of tokenization — tokenization for servicing (borrowing-base collateral, asset values, NAVs) and tokenization for collateralization (easier borrowing and lending against the asset) — and conflating them obscures where value is actually created.
insights.speaker: Anant (investments and product, Grove)
insights.so_what: Ask which of the two a given RWA product delivers; servicing tokenization sells to originators and banks, collateralization tokenization sells to lenders and allocators.

insights.claim: The blocker has shifted from lenders to originators: capital to lend on chain already exists, and what is missing is end-to-end originators who both originate assets on chain and borrow against them on chain.
insights.speaker: Anant (investments and product, Grove)
insights.so_what: Supply of on-chain-native collateral, not demand for it, is the bottleneck — origination platforms are the scarce asset in this value chain.
insights.quote: I mean I think the lenders are here. So I think what we're really looking for is that end to end originators to originate assets that are onchain and borrow against them onchain.

insights.claim: In 2022-2023 at BlockTower it was possible to codify the senior/junior side of an on-chain CLO but very hard to tokenize the underlying collateral, follow the pledge or monitor custody — infrastructure gaps that have closed materially in the past two to three years alongside maturing stablecoin on- and off-ramps.
insights.speaker: Anant (investments and product, Grove)
insights.so_what: The infrastructure maturity curve dates the thesis: what failed as an on-chain credit trade in 2022 may now be executable, which is why capital is re-entering the sector.

themes.theme: The BBVA facility as proof point

insights.claim: Fence Finance put a BBVA warehouse facility's loan agreement into software for a portfolio originating 300,000 loans per month, delivering real-time covenant and performance visibility on a book far past the point where spreadsheets can cope.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: A named tier-one bank running a live 300k-loans-per-month facility on this stack is the strongest available evidence that production adoption has started, not just piloting.

insights.claim: For an earned-wage-access originator with 10-25 day receivables, waiting a week for the bank's loan operations team to disburse would raise the cost of capital by roughly 60% — hundreds of thousands of dollars per facility — so BBVA won the mandate specifically because it could offer 'capital on demand'.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: Settlement speed is becoming a competitive weapon in warehouse lending mandates — banks without instant-disbursement tech will lose short-duration receivables business on price.
insights.quote: if they need to wait for one week until like the loan operations team in the bank uh disperses the money the the cost the cost of capital will be increased by around like 60%. So it's a crazy number.

insights.claim: The BBVA deployment saved roughly 80% of operational cost on both the bank's back/middle office and the fintech originator's side, cut 30-40% of total cost of capital, and seeded a business that has reached $1.5 billion in assets under administration.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: $1.5bn AUA is a concrete traction benchmark for the private-credit infrastructure category — track whether it compounds, since the savings are shared by both counterparties and should drive referral growth.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on institutional adoption is will rather than technology or law, because on-chain deals replicate existing legal structures rather than creating new ones — controllable electronic records, securities entitlements and depository tokens already exist and lawyers understand them.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: If regulation is not the gate, the catalyst to watch is deal flow, not rulemaking — a few large rated on-chain deals should unlock a fast follower wave.
insights.quote: The legal frameworks are here cuz and here's the key is we're not creating new structures. We're just replicating existing structures on chain. This is the rails, not the substance.

insights.claim: Issuing a private-credit asset as an NFT is a red flag because an NFT is not legally enforceable in court, unlike established wrappers such as controllable electronic records or securities entitlements.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: A fast negative screen for RWA deals: NFT-wrapped credit assets signal legal naivety and should be discounted heavily.
insights.quote: A board ape is not legally enforceable in a court of law. That's always a red flag for me when I hear people saying they're issuing an NFT.

insights.claim: Institutional adoption is a first-mover coordination problem — the industry is like penguins on an ice floe waiting for one to jump — and Fence's Montero independently frames it as everyone wanting to 'be first in being third'.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning and Juan Montero
insights.so_what: Expect adoption to be non-linear and reflexive: position ahead of the first large rated deal rather than waiting for gradual proof.
insights.quote: everyone in this industry likes to be first in being third and it's exactly that

insights.claim: All three panelists agree that most tokenization today is repackaging — putting a digital twin on chain — rather than genuine rebuilding, though Grove's Anant expects that to change within six to nine months.
insights.speaker: Anant, Juan Montero and Mike Manning
insights.so_what: Insiders concede the current RWA wave is mostly cosmetic; the six-to-nine-month window for natively on-chain issuance is the timeline to test the thesis against.
insights.quote: most organization is just repackaging putting a digital twin on chain

insights.claim: The on-chain credit industry is building leveraging platforms when it needs lending platforms — financing the real economy rather than merely levering existing assets.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: A critique that separates sustainable on-chain credit businesses from reflexive leverage stacks — favor platforms whose collateral originates from real-economy lending.
insights.quote: I think the industry right now is building leveraging platforms we need to start bringing building lending platforms we need to finance the real economy not just lever it up

insights.claim: Banks initially engaged with tokenization out of fear of missing out but are now adopting because it is genuinely better, and vendors deliberately hide the blockchain layer and sell only the benefits.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero and Mike Manning
insights.so_what: Successful enterprise blockchain go-to-market is now blockchain-invisible — a signal that product-led vendors will beat crypto-branded ones in institutional sales.
insights.quote: We're starting with fear. We're going to end way opportunity.

insights.claim: Underwriting and deal structuring should never be delegated to smart contracts, because they require judgment and bespoke flexibility — code should handle roughly 99% and flag the remaining 1% for humans.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning and Anant
insights.so_what: Draws the boundary of the addressable market: this is settlement and ops software, so credit-judgment franchises and their fee streams are not being disrupted.
insights.quote: This is a settlement and operational technology. It's not a judgment technology.

insights.claim: The prevailing 'opportunity through optionality' strategy of supporting 150-plus chains institutionalizes fragmentation, and the industry should instead pursue 'distribution through depth', consolidating around roughly five to six chains to build liquidity rather than optionality.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: If institutional RWA activity consolidates onto five or six chains, chain-level winner-take-most dynamics matter more than technical differentiation — position in the likely survivors.
insights.quote: It's not going to be one chain. It's not going to be 100. It's going to be something in the five to six range.

insights.claim: Institutions are increasingly indifferent to which chain an asset sits on but do care about who else is participating there, making critical mass of serious counterparties the real competitive moat for a blockchain.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Evaluate chains on the quality of institutional participants and ecosystem depth rather than throughput or fees.
insights.quote: Goldman will say they don't care what assets are on the chain but they do care who's in the room.

insights.claim: For value and cash movement, the decisive chain-selection criteria are resilience and uptime — avoiding single or few points of failure where a controlling party could stop paying for or turning against the service — plus security and ecosystem depth.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero and Anant
insights.so_what: Centralization risk is becoming an explicit procurement criterion for institutional chain selection, which disadvantages permissioned bank-owned chains over time.

insights.claim: Fence's position is that roughly 90-95% of what belongs on chain is money and asset flows, while items a smart contract cannot resolve — audited financial accounts, change-of-control covenants on the originator or servicer — must stay in the legal layer.
insights.speaker: Juan Montero (CEO, Fence Finance)
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for on-chain private credit: a hybrid legal-plus-code architecture, not full DeFi, which is also what makes it institutionally acceptable.
insights.quote: I think like what should be put into smart contracts is money flows and value flows. So money and asset flows that can be automated and that can happen like in 90% of the cases, 95% of the cases.

insights.claim: Manning disagrees with the hybrid ceiling and argues every life-cycle event including transferring the servicer from one smart contract to another can be executed on chain if properly defined in the legal documents.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: An open disagreement between an infrastructure vendor and a chain — the resolution determines how much of the servicing fee pool is actually automatable.

insights.claim: A facility's credit buy box can be encoded in a smart contract so that not-yet-originated future receivables are automatically accepted or rejected on arrival, answering the objection that on-chain rails cannot govern future receivable behavior.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Automated eligibility screening at the point of receivable intake is the mechanism that makes continuous borrowing-base management possible — the core technical claim to validate.

insights.claim: On-chain settlement can be asset-by-asset rather than gross or pool-level: a buy-now-pay-later consumer payment arriving as a stablecoin is applied directly to the individual loan, amortizing it and immediately pushing the stablecoin back out for redeployment into another loan.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Loan-level cash application is where capital efficiency beyond operational automation actually comes from, and it is also the fix for the reconciliation lag that hid the First Brands fraud.
insights.quote: It's getting applied directly against that one loan, not against the pool as a whole, but mapped to that particular loan

insights.claim: Personally identifiable information remains an unresolved constraint on what can go on chain in consumer-backed credit, which Manning concedes he cannot fully unpack.
insights.speaker: Mike Manning (head of institutional finance, Avalanche)
insights.so_what: Privacy tooling is an unsolved dependency for consumer ABS on chain — a gap that either constrains the addressable market or creates a venture opportunity.
